title: Tail latency (p99, p99.9) and coordinated omission
summary: Why averages hide slow requests, how fan-out turns rare leaf hiccups into common user delays, how closed-loop load testers omit the slow periods, and how to measure and tame the tail.
outcomes: Compute nearest-rank percentiles and explain why the mean and median hide tail latency
Compute how fan-out amplifies per-server tail probability with 1 - (1 - p)^N
Explain how closed-loop load generators cause coordinated omission and estimate its effect
Measure latency from intended start times (wrk2) and back-fill samples with HdrHistogram
Choose tail-tolerant techniques like hedged requests and aggregate latency via histograms

lessons.title: Why the average hides the requests users remember

blocks.md:
A latency **distribution** is the full set of response times your service produced in some window. Most dashboards squeeze it into one number, usually the mean. The trouble is that users do not experience the mean: each person experiences one particular request, and the slow ones are the ones they notice and complain about.

This course is about the slow end of that distribution, the **tail**, and about a measurement bug that makes the tail look far better than it is.

A **percentile** answers: below what latency do q percent of requests fall? We write p50 (the median), p99 (99th percentile) and p99.9. Using the nearest-rank rule, sort the n samples and take the one at rank $\lceil q \cdot n \rceil$.

So p99 = 250 ms means at least 99 requests in 100 took 250 ms or less, and only the slowest 1% could be worse. The tail is everything above a high percentile.

blocks.tex: p_q = x_{(\lceil q n \rceil)} \quad \text{where } x_{(1)} \le x_{(2)} \le \dots \le x_{(n)}
blocks.caption: Nearest-rank percentile: the k-th smallest sample, k = ceil(q n). Libraries differ in interpolation details, but the idea is the same.

scenes.caption: Twenty request latencies, sorted. Most sit between 4 and 10 ms. The mean is 19.25 ms, which is larger than 18 of the 20 samples, so no typical request looks like the mean.
p50 is the sample at rank ceil(0.5 x 20) = 10, which is 7 ms (index 9 because indices start at 0). Half the requests took 7 ms or less.
p90 is rank 18, so 15 ms. p95 is rank 19, so 40 ms. The step from p90 to p95 almost triples the latency: the tail is not a smooth continuation of the body.
p99 is rank ceil(19.8) = 20: the maximum, 210 ms. With only 20 samples, p99 is just the single worst request. You need many samples before a high percentile means anything.

blocks.md: With n samples you only have n(1 - q) samples above the q-th percentile. To say anything about p99.9 you need thousands of requests, and the estimate is driven by the handful of samples beyond it. Short benchmark runs cannot tell you about p99.9.

Two services can share the same mean and still behave completely differently. Service A answers all 100 requests in 10 ms. Service B answers 98 in 5 ms and 2 in 255 ms. Both have a mean of exactly 10 ms.

blocks.title: Same mean, different tail (100 requests each)

scenes.caption: Service A: every request takes 10 ms, so every statistic is 10 ms.
Service B: mean is still 10 ms and p50 through p98 look better than A (5 ms), but p99 and max are 255 ms. A dashboard showing only the mean or median would say B is the faster service.

blocks.prompt: Service B's p98 is 5 ms and its p99 is 255 ms. Would a 'p99 under 100 ms' alert fire, and would a 'mean under 20 ms' alert fire?
blocks.reveal: p99 is rank 99 of 100, which falls on the first of the two 255 ms requests, so the p99 alert fires. The mean alert does not fire: 10 ms is well under 20 ms. Two slow requests out of 100 are invisible to the mean and fully visible to p99.

blocks.md: Report latency as a distribution: several percentiles (p50, p99, p99.9) plus the maximum, not a mean. The mean blends a few terrible requests into many good ones and describes no actual user.

blocks.question: A service reports mean 12 ms and p50 8 ms. Which statement can you conclude?
options: At least half of requests took 8 ms or less, but you know nothing about how slow the worst 1% were
99% of requests took under 24 ms, because the tail is usually at most 2x the mean
The distribution is symmetric because mean and median are close
No request took longer than 12 ms on average, so p99 is at most 12 ms
blocks.explain: p50 = 8 ms means half the requests were at or below 8 ms. The mean being above the median hints at a right tail, but neither number bounds p99. One 5 second request among a million barely moves the mean. There is no rule that the tail is within 2x of the mean.

blocks.question: You run a 30 second benchmark at 20 requests per second (600 requests) and it prints p99.99 = 41 ms. How much should you trust that p99.99?
options: Fully, HdrHistogram style tools compute exact percentiles
Not much: 600 x 0.0001 = 0.06 samples lie above p99.99, so the value is just the maximum of this run
Somewhat: it is an average of the top 6 samples
Fully, as long as the mean is stable
blocks.explain: Nearest rank for q = 0.9999 and n = 600 is ceil(599.94) = 600, the maximum. The printout is exact for this data set but says nothing reliable about the service's true p99.99; rerun and it will move a lot. Collect far more samples, for example over longer runs.

lessons.title: Fan-out: why one server's p99 becomes everyone's problem

blocks.md:
Large services answer a user request by **fanning out**: a root server sends sub-requests to many leaf servers in parallel (search shards, cache nodes, microservices) and waits for all of them. The user request is only as fast as its slowest sub-request.

Dean and Barroso's paper *The Tail at Scale* (CACM 2013) uses a clean example: each server usually responds in 10 ms, but 1% of its responses take one second.

Recall from probability: if each leaf is slow independently with probability $p$, the chance that **none** of $N$ leaves is slow is $(1-p)^N$. So the chance that the user request is slow is the complement.

blocks.caption: Assumes leaves are independent. Correlated slowness (a shared switch, a synchronized GC) changes the numbers but not the lesson.

blocks.md: Plug in the paper's case, $p = 0.01$ and $N = 100$: $1 - 0.99^{100} = 0.634$. **63% of user requests take over one second**, even though each server is slow only 1% of the time. The paper also notes that with one-in-10,000 slow responses and 2,000 servers, $1 - 0.9999^{2000} = 0.181$, almost one user request in five is slow.

blocks.title: Chance a fan-out request hits at least one slow leaf

scenes.caption: Each leaf is slow 1% of the time (its p99 is the slow value). At N = 1 the user sees 1% slow requests; by N = 100 it is 63%, and by a few hundred leaves nearly every request is slow.
Cut the per-leaf rate tenfold to 0.1%. At N = 100 the user still sees 9.5% slow requests, and at N = 1000 it climbs back to 63%.
At 0.01% per leaf (a leaf p99.99 problem), N = 100 gives 1.0% slow requests and N = 2000 gives 18%. With wide fan-out, a leaf's p99.99 becomes the service's p99.

blocks.prompt: Your root fans out to 100 leaves and you want at most 1% of user requests to be slow. What fraction of leaf responses may be slow?
blocks.reveal: Solve $1 - (1-p)^{100} \le 0.01$, so $p \le 1 - 0.99^{1/100} \approx 0.0001$. Each leaf must be slow at most about **1 time in 10,000**. In other words, to hit a p99 target at the service you must hit that latency at roughly p99.99 on every leaf. This is why teams with deep fan-out track p99.9 and p99.99, not just p99.

blocks.md: This is not only a model. The paper reports measurements from a real Google service whose root fans out through intermediate servers to many leaves. For one random leaf request the 99th percentile was 10 ms. For the root to collect **all** leaf responses, the 99th percentile was 140 ms, and waiting for just 95% of the leaves had a p99 of 70 ms. The slowest 5% of leaves account for half of the total p99.

blocks.title: Measured leaf finishing times (Tail at Scale, Table 1)

scenes.caption: Median (p50) finishing time measured at the root: 1 ms for one leaf, 12 ms to get 95% of leaves, 40 ms to get all of them.
p95: 5 ms, 32 ms and 87 ms. Waiting for the stragglers dominates.
p99: 10 ms, 70 ms and 140 ms. The last 5% of leaves double the p99, which is why the paper's techniques target those slow outliers.

blocks.md: The same arithmetic applies inside a single page. If loading one page makes 40 backend calls, each with a 1% chance of hitting its p99 latency, then $1 - 0.99^{40} = 0.331$: about a third of page loads include at least one p99-or-worse call. Your p99 is not a rare event for users; it is a routine one.
With fan-out N, the user-visible tail is set by roughly the 1 - 1/(100N) quantile of each component, not by its p99. The wider the fan-out, the deeper into the tail you must measure and engineer.

blocks.question: A leaf service has p99 = 50 ms and p99.9 = 400 ms. A new feature makes each user request fan out to 10 of these leaves instead of 1. Roughly what fraction of user requests now see at least one leaf response of 400 ms or more?
options: About 0.1%, same as before, because each leaf is unchanged
About 1%, since 1 - 0.999^10 is roughly 10 x 0.1%
About 10%, since 10 leaves times 1%
About 63%
blocks.explain: Each leaf is at or above 400 ms with probability 0.001. P(at least one of 10) = 1 - 0.999^10 = 0.00996, about 1%. The user-level p99 is now around 400 ms instead of 50 ms. For small p, 1 - (1-p)^N is close to N p.

blocks.question: Why does fan-out make tail latency matter more than median latency for the user?
options: Because the root averages the leaf latencies, and averages are dominated by outliers
Because leaves process requests serially
Because the user waits for the slowest of N responses, so a rare per-leaf event becomes a common per-request event
Because median latency cannot be measured at the root
blocks.explain: The root waits for the maximum, not the mean, of the leaf latencies. The probability that the maximum includes a tail event grows as 1 - (1-p)^N.

lessons.title: Coordinated omission: the load tester stops looking when it hurts

blocks.md: Now the measurement problem. Most load generators are **closed-loop**: each connection sends a request, waits for the response, then sends the next. Schroeder, Wierman and Harchol-Balter (NSDI 2006) call this a *closed system model*: new arrivals are triggered only by completions. Real users of a public service behave more like an *open* model: they arrive whether or not the server is keeping up.

This bug is called **coordinated omission**; Gil Tene's wrk2 README describes it in detail. When the server stalls, a closed-loop tester is stuck waiting on the stalled request, so it does not send (and does not measure) the requests it would have sent during the stall. The tester coordinates with the server: it politely backs off exactly when the server is slow, and the slow period is omitted from the data.

Let us watch it happen on a tiny example.

blocks.title: One connection, one request every 10 ms, a 60 ms server stall

scenes.caption: Simplified model: the tester plans a request every 10 ms on one connection; each takes 2 ms. Requests at 0 and 10 ms finish at 2 and 12 ms. Both record 2 ms.

At 20 ms the server freezes for 60 ms (think GC pause or a stopped process). The request sent at 20 ms finishes at 82 ms and records 62 ms. Meanwhile the tester is blocked, so the requests planned for 30, 40, 50, 60, 70 and 80 ms are never sent.

The tester resumes at its next slot, 90 ms, and records 2 ms three more times. Final data: 6 samples, 5 of them 2 ms and one 62 ms. Median 2 ms. The stall that covered half the run is one sample in six.

Real users do not wait for each other. Each arrives on schedule and queues in arrival order (2 ms each). The user at 30 ms finishes at 84 (54 ms), at 50 finishes at 88 (38 ms), at 70 at 92 (22 ms), at 90 at 96 (6 ms). Five of the twelve users are shown.

blocks.md: Line up the two data sets. The closed-loop tester recorded 6 samples: `2 2 62 2 2 2`. The twelve users who arrived on the planned schedule experienced `2 2 62 54 46 38 30 22 14 6 2 2`. Seven of those twelve (58%) waited more than 10 ms; the tester saw one of six (17%).

blocks.title: What the tester reports vs what users experienced

scenes.caption: Closed-loop tester, 6 samples: median 2 ms, p75 2 ms, mean 12 ms, max 62 ms. Looks like a fast service with one hiccup.
Users on the planned schedule, 12 samples: median 14 ms, p75 38 ms, mean 23.3 ms, max 62 ms. Only the max agrees, and the median is 7x worse than reported.

blocks.md: Coordinated omission does not make individual samples wrong: the 2 ms readings were real. The bug is which samples exist. The tester samples less often precisely when the server is slow, so the sample set is biased toward good moments. No statistic computed afterwards can recover samples that were never taken.

The HdrHistogram README gives a starker version. Sample a system every 10 ms. It answers in 1 ms for 100 seconds (10,000 samples), then freezes for 100 seconds, during which a closed-loop sampler records a single 100 second sample. In the raw data, 10,000 of 10,001 samples (99.99%) are 1 ms, so every percentile up to p99.99 reads 1 ms.

blocks.prompt: In that scenario, a user arriving at a random moment during the 200 seconds has what chance of waiting longer than 1 ms, and what would an honest p75 be?
blocks.reveal: Half of the wall-clock time was the freeze, so a random arrival has a **50%** chance of hitting it. If you add the requests that should have been issued every 10 ms during the freeze (each would have waited until the freeze ended: 99.99 s, 99.98 s, down to 10 ms), the data set has 20,000 samples, exactly half of them 1 ms. Then p75 is **50 seconds**, p90 is 80 s and p99 is 98 s, against 1 ms in the raw data.

blocks.title: HdrHistogram README scenario: raw vs corrected

scenes.caption: Raw closed-loop data (10,001 samples): p50 through p99 are all 0.001 s (1 ms) and the mean is 0.011 s. The 100 second freeze is a single outlier.
With the 9,999 missing samples restored (20,000 samples): p50 is still 1 ms, but p75 is 50 s, p90 is 80 s, p99 is 98 s and the mean is 25 s. This matches what a random user would see.

blocks.question: A closed-loop benchmark with 50 connections reports p99 = 4 ms. During the run the server had a 2 second GC pause. Which is the most likely truth?
options: p99 is about 4 ms; the pause produced at most 50 slow samples and those are correctly counted
The true p99 for users arriving at a constant rate is likely far higher, because requests that should have been sent during the pause were never sent or measured
p99 is lower than 4 ms because the pause reduced load
Percentiles are unaffected by coordinated omission; only the mean is
blocks.explain: Each of the 50 connections recorded one long sample during the pause and then nothing until it resumed. A constant-rate workload would have issued many requests during those 2 seconds, each waiting out the pause. Those are missing, so the reported p99 is biased low. wrk2's README shows a 1.4 s pause turning p99 from 6.04 ms (uncorrected) into 1.27 s.

blocks.question: Which change to a closed-loop tester does NOT fix coordinated omission?
options: Measuring each request from the time the schedule says it should have been sent
Sending requests on a fixed schedule from independent senders that never wait for responses
Adding more connections so that each one blocks less often
Back-filling the missing samples using a known expected interval between requests
blocks.explain: More connections reduce the effect but every connection still stops sending while it waits, so the bias remains (the NSDI paper notes closed systems approach open ones only slowly as concurrency grows). Measuring from intended start, open-loop sending, and interval-based back-fill all restore the missing samples.

lessons.title: Measuring correctly: intended start times and HdrHistogram

blocks.md: The fix is to measure latency from when the request **should** have been sent, not when it actually was. That requires a *plan*: a schedule of intended send times, for example one request every $1/R$ seconds at rate $R$. wrk2, Gil Tene's fork of the wrk HTTP benchmark, does exactly this: it generates a constant throughput given by `-R` (or `--rate`) and records latency from the planned send time.

Why does that work even on a single blocking connection? If a reply comes back late, the next intended send time is already in the past, so the loop sends immediately, and the time it spent waiting to send is charged to that request. The queueing delay the tester itself suffered is exactly what a real user arriving on schedule would have suffered.

blocks.title: Same stall as before, measured two ways
blocks.code:
interval = 10                       # ms between planned sends
start = now()
for i in range(12):
    intended = start + i * interval
    sleep_until(intended)           # returns at once if already late
    sent = now()
    call(server)                    # blocks until the reply
    done = now()
    naive.record(done - sent)       # coordinated omission
    fixed.record(done - intended)   # wrk2 style

scenes.caption: Request 0 is planned at 0 ms, sent at 0, done at 2. Both recorders get 2 ms.
Request 2 is sent on time at 20 ms but the server stalls until 80, so it is done at 82. Both recorders get 62 ms; so far they agree.
Request 3 was planned for 30 ms. sleep_until returns immediately because it is already 82. Sent at 82, done at 84. Naive records 2 ms; fixed records 84 - 30 = 54 ms.
The loop keeps catching up 2 ms at a time. Request 9 (planned 90) is sent at 94, done at 96: naive 2 ms, fixed 6 ms. Request 10 is back on schedule.

After 12 requests. naive: eleven 2 ms samples and one 62 ms (median 2). This loop catches up instead of skipping slots, yet the stall is still one sample. fixed: matches the open-loop users (median 14 ms, 7 of 12 over 10 ms).

blocks.md: Latency = completion time minus *intended* start time. The intended start comes from a load plan that does not depend on how fast the server answers.

wrk2's README shows the effect on a real Apache server at 2,000 requests per second with 100 connections. It reports both its corrected histogram and an uncorrected one (`--u_latency`). On a quiet run the uncorrected p99 was 5.43 ms against 10.52 ms corrected, about 2x. In a second run the author paused the server process for about 1.4 seconds with Ctrl-Z.

blocks.title: wrk2 README, run with a 1.4 s pause (2000 req/s)

scenes.caption: Uncorrected (measured from actual send): p50 3.02 ms, p90 4.87 ms, p99 6.04 ms. Only p99.9 (1410 ms) hints at the pause.
Corrected (from intended send): p50 8.61, p90 11.77, p99 1270 ms, p99.9 1420 ms. The p99 is 210x the uncorrected one.

blocks.md: Sometimes you cannot control sending, for example when instrumenting an existing loop that samples every 10 ms. **HdrHistogram** (Gil Tene's High Dynamic Range histogram, which wrk2 uses for lossless recording) offers `recordValueWithExpectedInterval(value, interval)`. If a value exceeds the expected interval, it also records the samples that would have been taken during that time, each one interval smaller, down to the interval itself.

blocks.caption: The back-fill loop from the HdrHistogram Java source.

blocks.title: Back-filling the 62 ms sample with interval 10 ms

scenes.caption: Top row: what the users planned at 20, 30, ..., 90 ms actually waited. A naive recorder holds only the one 62 ms sample from the stalled request.
recordValueWithExpectedInterval(62, 10) adds 52, 42, 32, 22 and 12, stopping before 2 because 2 is below the interval. Six samples in place of one.

Close to the truth but not identical: the back-fill assumes the missing requests would have finished the moment the stall ended, ignoring their own service time and queueing. It is an estimate, which is why a real load plan is better.

blocks.md: HdrHistogram also matters for recording itself. It keeps counts in buckets whose width scales with the value, configured by a number of significant digits. The README's example tracks 1 microsecond to 1 hour at 3 significant digits (each value quantized to within 0.1%) in a fixed footprint of around 185 KB, so you can record every request instead of sampling, and still read any percentile afterwards.

Run constant-rate tests at several rates up to and past expected capacity, and long enough to collect samples beyond the percentiles you care about. wrk2's README notes its latencies are accurate to about plus or minus 1 ms because of OS sleep granularity, and that its 10 second calibration makes runs shorter than 10 to 20 seconds unreliable.

blocks.question: Spot the bug in this load loop: `t0 = now(); send(req); resp = recv(); hist.record(now() - t0)` run back to back on 16 connections.
options: It records in milliseconds instead of microseconds
It measures from actual send time on closed-loop connections, so requests delayed while the connection was blocked are never counted
It should use the mean instead of a histogram
Nothing, 16 connections make it open-loop
blocks.explain: Each connection only sends after the previous reply, and t0 is taken at actual send. Time a request spent waiting to be sent during a stall is invisible. Fix: drive sends from a rate plan and record now() minus the intended send time.

blocks.question: You can only sample a queue's latency once every 100 ms from a monitoring thread that blocks while sampling. One sample reads 1,050 ms. With recordValueWithExpectedInterval(1050, 100), how many values are recorded in total?
blocks.explain: It records 1050, then 950, 850, ..., 150: the loop continues while the value is at least 100, so it stops before 50. That is 1 + 9 = 10 values.

lessons.title: Taming the tail: hedged requests and honest reporting

blocks.md: Measuring the tail correctly is half the job. *The Tail at Scale* argues that in large shared clusters you cannot eliminate every source of variability: shared resources, background daemons, garbage collection (both language GC and SSD garbage collection), maintenance like log compaction, power management, and queueing at many layers. Instead, build **tail-tolerant** systems that make a predictable whole out of less predictable parts.

First, reduce variability where you can. The paper lists keeping low-level queues short so higher-level priority policies take effect, splitting long requests into smaller ones to avoid head-of-line blocking, and throttling or synchronizing background work. For wide fan-out, running background activity in a brief burst on all machines at once slows only the requests in that burst, instead of having some machine always busy and stretching every request's tail.

Second, work around it with replicas. A **hedged request** sends the request to one replica and, if no reply arrives within a short delay, sends a copy to another replica and takes whichever answers first, cancelling the rest. Waiting until the 95th-percentile expected latency before hedging limits extra load to about 5%.

scenes.caption: The client sends the request to its preferred replica, A, and starts a timer at the hedge delay (here 15 ms in our toy model).
A happens to be in a slow episode (GC, a busy disk). The timer fires with no reply, so the client sends a copy to B.
B answers 10 ms later, at 25 ms total. The client uses it and cancels A's copy so it stops wasting work.

blocks.md: Let us quantify it with a simplified toy model: each replica answers in 10 ms with probability 0.99 and in 1,000 ms with probability 0.01, independently. Hedge after 15 ms. A single request is now slow only if both replicas are slow: probability $0.01^2 = 0.0001$. Otherwise it takes 10 ms (99%) or 25 ms (0.99%). Only the 1% of requests that miss the deadline send a second copy, so extra load is 1%.

blocks.prompt: Put that hedged leaf behind a fan-out of 100. Without hedging, 63% of user requests are slow, so even the median is 1,000 ms. What is the user p99 with hedging?
blocks.reveal: Each leaf is now slow with probability 0.0001, so P(any of 100 slow) = $1 - 0.9999^{100} \approx 0.0099$. That is just under 1%, so p99 drops to **25 ms**. But p99.9 is still 1,000 ms: hedging pushes the tail out, it does not remove it.

blocks.title: Toy model: fan-out of 100, with and without hedging

scenes.caption: No hedging: only 36.6% of user requests avoid every slow leaf, so p50, p90, p99 and p99.9 are all 1,000 ms.
Hedging at 15 ms (1% extra requests): p50, p90 and p99 are 25 ms, p99.9 is still 1,000 ms. Simplified: real slow episodes are often correlated across replicas, which weakens the gain.

blocks.md: The paper reports a real benchmark: reading 1,000 keys spread over 100 BigTable servers, hedging after 10 ms cut the 99.9th-percentile latency from 1,800 ms to 74 ms while sending just 2% more requests. A refinement, **tied requests**, enqueues the request on two servers at once and lets whichever starts first tell the other to cancel.

Percentiles do not average. Server X serves 900 requests all at 10 ms (p99 10 ms); server Y serves 100 requests, 20 of them at 400 ms (p99 400 ms). The average of the two p99s is 205 ms, but the combined 1,000 requests have p99 = 400 ms: 20 slow requests is 2% of the total. Prometheus's docs make the same point: precomputed quantiles cannot be aggregated, but histogram bucket counts can be summed.

Honest tail reporting: record every request into a mergeable histogram (HdrHistogram or bucketed histograms), measure from intended start under a load plan, merge histograms rather than percentiles across machines, and report several high percentiles plus the max, with the sample count.

blocks.question: Your team wants a fleet-wide p99 dashboard. Each of 40 hosts exports its own p99 every minute. What should you do?
options: Average the 40 p99 values, weighting by request count
Take the maximum of the 40 p99 values, which is exactly the fleet p99
Export histogram bucket counts from each host, sum them, and compute p99 from the merged histogram
Take the median of the 40 p99 values to ignore outlier hosts
blocks.explain: Percentiles are not additive; neither the weighted mean nor the max of per-host p99s equals the fleet p99 in general. Summed histogram counts describe the combined distribution, so the percentile computed from them is right up to bucket resolution.

blocks.question: Hedging after the p95 expected latency costs about 5% extra load. Why not hedge immediately (send to two replicas at time 0) to cut the tail further?
options: It would double the load, raising queueing and utilization so much that latency for everyone can get worse
It is forbidden by TCP
It would not reduce latency at all
Replicas cannot answer the same request twice
blocks.explain: Sending every request twice doubles the work. Higher utilization lengthens queues, a main source of tail latency. Waiting for a high-percentile delay hedges only the requests likely to be stuck, giving most of the benefit for a few percent extra load; tied requests with cancellation are another way to keep the overhead small.

blocks.question: A colleague says: 'Our load test with wrk2 at 5,000 requests per second shows p99 = 900 ms but production p99 at the same traffic is 20 ms, so wrk2 must be broken.' What is the most likely explanation to check first?
options: HdrHistogram rounds values up by 45x
Production percentiles are always lower than test percentiles
wrk2 sends requests twice
wrk2 measures from intended send times, so if the server cannot sustain 5,000 req/s, queueing builds up and is honestly reported; check that the achieved rate matched the target
blocks.explain: If the requested rate exceeds what the system can serve, the backlog grows during the run and every request's latency since its intended time keeps rising. Compare the reported Requests/sec to the -R target and check the test setup (for example, one client machine as bottleneck) before blaming the tool.
